questions.question: Design a library management system. What are the key classes?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you identify core domain entities and distinguish between catalog abstraction (Book) versus physical instances (BookItem) in inventory management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often collapse Book and BookItem into one class, missing that one book title can have multiple physical copies with independent states
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the one-to-many relationship between Book and BookItem and mention how BookItem tracks location (shelf number) and condition separately

questions.direct_answer: A library management system needs entities for catalog (Book), physical inventory (BookItem), users (Member, Librarian), and transactions (BookLending, Reservation, Fine). The key distinction is Book represents the catalog entry while BookItem represents each physical copy with its own barcode and availability status.

items: Book: catalog record (ISBN, title, authors, genre) — conceptual
BookItem: physical copy (barcode, current status, location) — physical
Member: borrower with member ID, borrow limit, current checked-out items
BookLending: transaction (who borrowed which copy when)
Reservation: member reserves a book when all copies are checked out
Fine: tracks overdue fines per member

answer_sections.content: The key design insight is separating Book (catalog concept) from BookItem (physical copy). A library has one record for 'Clean Code by Robert Martin' but 5 physical copies. When you checkout, you're checking out a BookItem, not the Book. Each BookItem has a barcode, current status (AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT, RESERVED), and a due date when checked out. The Member entity has a maximum borrow limit and a list of current loans. BookLending is the transaction record — created when a book is checked out, completed when returned. This models the real domain accurately: you can search for a Book, see how many copies are available, and reserve one if all are out.

follow_up_questions: How would you handle the reservation queue when a book is returned?
How do you calculate overdue fines in your design?

speakable_v2.hook: Library management is the parking lot problem in disguise — but with one twist that trips up almost every beginner.

beats.text: A library system models catalog records, physical copies, borrowing transactions, and member management. The key insight is that there are two representations of every book.

groups.heading: Book vs BookItem
groups.text: Book is the catalog record — ISBN, title, authors. BookItem is a physical copy — barcode, status (AVAILABLE / CHECKED_OUT / RESERVED), current due date. One Book can have many BookItems.

groups.heading: Member
groups.text: Has a member ID, a borrow limit, and a list of current loans. Can't borrow if they have outstanding fines.

groups.heading: BookLending
groups.text: The transaction record: which BookItem, which Member, checkout date, due date, return date. Created on checkout, updated on return.

groups.heading: Reservation and Fine
groups.text: Reservation holds a FIFO queue of members waiting for a book. Fine tracks overdue fees per member.

beats.text: candidates miss: the Book vs BookItem split. Without it you can't track which physical copy is where, or handle multiple copies of the same title. Always separate the catalog concept from the physical object.

speakable_v2.cap: Book is the catalog entry; BookItem is the physical copy. That one distinction unlocks the whole library design.
followup_handoff: How do you handle the reservation queue when a book is returned?
How do you calculate overdue fines?

sections.title: Core Entity Model for Library Management
sections.content: A library management system models two parallel hierarchies: **catalog entities** (what books exist) and **physical entities** (actual copies on shelves). The **Book** class represents a catalog entry—title, author, ISBN, genre—shared by all copies. Each physical copy is a **BookItem** with its own barcode, condition, and shelf location. **Member** and **Librarian** are user types with different permissions. **BookLending** captures a checkout transaction linking a Member to a BookItem with issue and due dates. **Reservation** queues members waiting for a book. **Fine** tracks overdue penalties. This separation of catalog from inventory is crucial: when a member searches for "Clean Code," they find one Book entry, but the system checks if any of its five BookItems are available. This mirrors real library operations where one title has multiple copies.

sections.title: Key Classes with Relationships
Key Points
content: **Book vs BookItem separation**: Book is catalog metadata (title, author), BookItem is the physical copy with barcode and shelf location. One-to-many relationship.
**BookLending as transaction**: Captures who borrowed what when, not just a boolean flag. Essential for audit trail and fine calculation.
**Member vs Librarian roles**: Members borrow and reserve; Librarians issue books, process returns, and manage inventory. Different permission sets.
**Reservation entity**: Tracks waiting queue per book. When a BookItem returns, first Reservation in queue gets notified.
**Fine calculation**: Based on BookLending dates. Fine = (return date - due date) × daily rate if overdue. Outstanding fines block new borrowing.
**Status tracking**: BookItem status (AVAILABLE, LOANED, RESERVED, LOST) drives availability checks. Status transitions happen during issue/return operations.
**Immutability with records**: Using Java records for entities ensures thread-safety and clear value semantics for domain objects like Book and BookItem.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd design the library system around five core entities. First is Book, which represents a catalog entry with title, author, and ISBN. Then there's BookItem, which is each physical copy with its own barcode and shelf location. The key distinction here is that one Book can have multiple BookItems—like five copies of Clean Code on different shelves. For users, I'd have Member and Librarian with different permissions. Members can borrow and reserve, while Librarians handle issuing and returns. Next is BookLending, which records a checkout transaction: which member took which BookItem, when it's due, and when it was returned. This isn't just a boolean flag—it's a full transaction record we need for calculating fines. Reservation queues members waiting for a book, and Fine tracks overdue penalties. The common mistake freshers make is merging Book and BookItem into one class. That breaks down when you realize you need to track that copy three of a book is on loan while copy five is available. You also can't calculate fines without the lending transaction dates. In an interview, I'd sketch these classes with their relationships on a whiteboard, showing the one-to-many from Book to BookItem, and explain how BookLending connects Member to BookItem with timestamps. That shows you understand both the domain model and how real libraries work.

questions.question: How do you handle the book reservation system in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you model ordered waitlists and implement the Observer pattern to handle asynchronous notification when inventory becomes available
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often use a simple list without FIFO ordering or forget to notify waiting members when a book returns, breaking the reservation flow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention expiration timers—if the notified member doesn't pick up the book within 24 hours, move to the next reservation in queue

questions.direct_answer: Use a queue per Book to store Reservations in order. When a Member reserves, append to the queue. On BookItem return, the Book checks its reservation queue and notifies the first Member. Implement Observer pattern where BookItem notifies Book of status changes, and Book processes the next pending Reservation.

answer_sections.content: When all copies of a book are checked out, members can join a reservation queue. The queue is on the Book entity. When a BookItem is returned, it notifies the Book. Book checks if there's a reservation — if yes, it processes the reservation: assigns the returned BookItem to the first member in queue and sends them a notification. Observer pattern works naturally here: BookItem is the observable, Book (or ReservationManager) is the observer. The notification to the member (email/SMS) can be an event published to a notification service — keeping the library domain clean and not mixing notification infrastructure into domain classes.

follow_up_questions: How long should a reservation be held before expiring?
What data structure is best for the reservation queue and why?

beats.text: When all copies of a book are checked out, members join a reservation queue. The queue lives on the Book entity. When any BookItem is returned, the queue is processed.

items: Book holds a Queue of Reservation objects — FIFO ensures fairness
When a member reserves, add a new Reservation to the queue
When a BookItem is returned, notify the Book via Observer
Book polls the queue: if someone's waiting, assign the returned BookItem to them
Send the member a notification — but keep notification logic out of the domain class

beats.text: Observer pattern: BookItem is the observable. On return, it calls onBookItemReturned() on the Book. Book processes the head of its reservation queue and fires a ReservationAvailableEvent for the notification service to handle.
non-obvious: keep email and SMS notification logic out of the Book class. Publish an event and let a separate notification service consume it. This keeps your domain model clean and testable.

speakable_v2.cap: Queue on Book for FIFO fairness. Observer to trigger it on return. Fire an event for notifications — don't put email logic in your domain class.

sections.title: Queue-Based Reservation with Observer Pattern
sections.content: A **reservation system** manages fairness when all copies of a book are loaned out. Members join a **waiting queue** per Book in FIFO order. When any BookItem of that Book is returned, the system must notify the first member in the queue. This is a classic **Observer pattern** application: BookItem (subject) notifies Book (observer) of status changes, and Book processes its reservation queue. The queue ensures fairness—members are served in request order, not randomly. The flow: Member requests reservation → system checks if all BookItems are loaned → if yes, add Reservation to Book's queue. On return, BookItem changes status to AVAILABLE and fires a notification. Book receives the event, peeks the first Reservation, and sends an email or SMS to that Member. If the member picks up within 24 hours, remove the reservation. If not, expire it and notify the next in queue. This decouples the return process from reservation logic—the person returning a book doesn't need to know about waiting members.

sections.title: Observer Pattern for Reservation Queue
Key Points
content: **Queue per Book**: Each Book maintains a reservation queue (LinkedList or PriorityQueue). Members are served in FIFO order ensuring fairness.
**Observer pattern**: BookItem acts as subject, Book as observer. On return, BookItem calls book.onBookItemReturned() to trigger reservation processing.
**Prevent unnecessary reservations**: Check if any BookItem is available before allowing reservation. Reservations only make sense when all copies are loaned.
**Notification mechanism**: When a BookItem returns, peek the first Reservation and send notification (email/SMS) to the waiting member.
**Expiration timer**: If notified member doesn't pick up within 24 hours, mark reservation expired and process the next in queue automatically.
**Decoupling**: The member returning a book doesn't know about reservations. Book class encapsulates all reservation logic, keeping BookItem simple.
**Race condition handling**: Use synchronized blocks or locks when multiple BookItems of the same Book return simultaneously to avoid duplicate notifications.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd use a queue to handle reservations, with one queue per Book. When a member tries to borrow a book and all copies are loaned out, they can reserve it. We add a Reservation to the Book's queue in FIFO order. That way, the first person to reserve gets the book first when it comes back. The interesting part is the notification flow. I'd use the Observer pattern here. When someone returns a BookItem, it doesn't directly check reservations—that'd be tight coupling. Instead, the BookItem notifies its parent Book that it's been returned. The Book receives this notification, looks at its reservation queue, and if there's someone waiting, sends them an email or SMS saying the book is ready. Then I'd add an expiration rule. Once notified, the member has 24 hours to pick it up. If they don't, we mark that reservation as expired and automatically notify the next person in the queue. The common mistake is using a plain list instead of a queue, which loses the ordering, or forgetting to notify members at all. In a real system, you'd also need to handle race conditions—what if two copies of the same book return at the same time? You'd use a lock on the reservation queue to ensure only one notification goes out. That shows you're thinking beyond just the happy path.

questions.question: How do you model search functionality in the library system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you apply the Strategy pattern to decouple search implementation from the catalog interface, demonstrating knowledge of behavioral design patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers hardcode multiple search methods in LibraryCatalog (searchByTitle, searchByAuthor) creating a bloated class that violates Open-Closed Principle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention combining criteria with Composite pattern for advanced searches like "author AND genre" or suggest indexing strategies for performance

questions.direct_answer: Use the Strategy pattern with a SearchCriteria interface. Implementations like SearchByTitle, SearchByAuthor, SearchByISBN, SearchByGenre encapsulate different search algorithms. LibraryCatalog accepts any SearchCriteria and delegates to its execute method. This keeps search logic decoupled and makes adding new criteria trivial.

answer_sections.content: For search, I use the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with one method: matches(Book). Each search type is a separate implementation: TitleSearchCriteria, AuthorSearchCriteria, ISBNCriteria, GenreCriteria. The catalog's search method takes any SearchCriteria — it doesn't know or care which one. This makes the design open for extension: adding a SearchByPublicationYear requires a new class, no changes to catalog. You can also compose criteria: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')) for multi-field search. This is the Specification pattern used in DDD, and it maps cleanly to database queries if you extend it.

follow_up_questions: How would you add full-text search to the library catalog?
What is the Specification pattern and how does it relate to this design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: Search sounds simple until you need to search by title, author, ISBN, and genre — and combine them. Strategy pattern handles all of that cleanly.

beats.text: Library search uses the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with a single matches(Book) method. Each search type is a separate implementation. The catalog's search method accepts any SearchCriteria.

items: SearchCriteria interface: boolean matches(Book book)
TitleSearchCriteria: checks if title contains the query (case-insensitive)
AuthorSearchCriteria: checks if any author name matches
ISBNSearchCriteria: exact match on ISBN
AndCriteria: composes two criteria — both must match

beats.text: To search for a Java book by Joshua Bloch: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')). Adding a new search type — like SearchByPublicationYear — is a new class, not a change to LibraryCatalog.
non-obvious: this pattern is called the Specification pattern in Domain-Driven Design. If an interviewer asks about Specification, this is the answer — it's Strategy applied to filtering predicates.

speakable_v2.cap: SearchCriteria interface + one class per search type + composable with AndCriteria. Open for extension, zero changes to the catalog.
followup_handoff: How would you add full-text search?

sections.title: Strategy Pattern for Flexible Search
sections.content: **Search functionality** in a library needs to support multiple dimensions: title, author, ISBN, genre, publication year. Hardcoding methods like searchByTitle(), searchByAuthor() in LibraryCatalog creates a bloated class that violates the **Open-Closed Principle**—every new search type requires modifying the catalog. The **Strategy pattern** solves this by extracting search logic into separate classes. Define a **SearchCriteria** interface with an execute method that takes the book collection and returns matches. Concrete implementations like **SearchByTitle** or **SearchByAuthor** encapsulate their filtering logic. The LibraryCatalog now has a single search(SearchCriteria) method that delegates to the strategy. Adding a new search type means creating a new class, not changing existing code. This pattern also enables **composite searches**: combine multiple criteria with AND/OR logic. For example, "books by Martin Fowler in the Software category" uses two strategies chained together. The analogy: search criteria are like interchangeable camera lenses—each focuses differently, but all fit the same camera body (the catalog).

sections.title: Strategy Pattern for Search Implementation
Key Points
content: **Strategy pattern extraction**: Define SearchCriteria interface with execute method. Each search type (title, author, ISBN) becomes a separate class implementing this interface.
**Single search method**: LibraryCatalog has one search(SearchCriteria) method instead of multiple searchByX methods. This keeps the catalog class lean.
**Open-Closed Principle**: Adding new search types means creating new classes, not modifying LibraryCatalog. Closed for modification, open for extension.
**Composite searches**: Combine multiple criteria with AND/OR logic. SearchByAuthorAndGenre wraps two strategies and applies both filters sequentially.
**Case-insensitive matching**: Convert search terms and book fields to lowercase for user-friendly matching. ISBN searches are exact since they're unique identifiers.
**Performance consideration**: For large catalogs, use indexed maps (HashMap by ISBN, TreeMap by author) instead of linear streams. Strategy classes then query indexes.
**Null safety**: Use Optional<Book> for single results like ISBN search. For multi-result searches, return empty list instead of null to avoid NullPointerException.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd use the Strategy pattern to keep search flexible. The key idea is to avoid hardcoding methods like searchByTitle, searchByAuthor in the LibraryCatalog class. That approach creates a bloated class and violates the Open-Closed Principle—every time you want to add a new search type, you modify the catalog. Instead, I'd create a SearchCriteria interface with an execute method that takes the book collection and returns matching books. Then I'd implement concrete strategies like SearchByTitle, SearchByAuthor, SearchByISBN, each with its own filtering logic. The LibraryCatalog now has just one method: search that accepts any SearchCriteria and delegates to it. This makes adding new search types trivial—just create a new class, no changes to existing code. For example, if you later want to search by publication year, you write SearchByYear and you're done. You can also combine criteria for advanced searches. Imagine searching for books by Martin Fowler in the Software genre. You'd create a CompositeSearchCriteria that chains two strategies together with AND logic. The common mistake is putting all search logic directly in the catalog class, which becomes unmaintainable as requirements grow. In a production system, I'd also mention indexing—for large catalogs, you'd use HashMaps keyed by ISBN or author name instead of streaming through every book. That's a performance optimization the Strategy pattern doesn't prevent.

questions.question: How do you handle fines in the library management system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you handle temporal calculations and state management for financial transactions, showing understanding of date arithmetic and business rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often calculate fine as a simple subtraction without handling edge cases like partial days, weekends, or grace periods, or fail to block borrowing for outstanding fines
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention grace period (first day free), weekend/holiday exclusion from fine calculation, or progressive fine rates (higher after 30 days overdue)

questions.direct_answer: Calculate fine during book return by comparing return date to due date. If overdue, fine equals overdue days multiplied by daily rate. Use a FineCalculator strategy to encapsulate rate logic (standard, premium members might have different rates). Member entity tracks outstanding fine balance that must be cleared before new borrowing is allowed.

answer_sections.content: Fine calculation is straightforward: when a book is returned, compare the return date to the due date on the BookLending record. If return date > due date, calculate overdueDays and multiply by the daily rate. I use a FineCalculator Strategy so the rate and calculation method can change without modifying the checkout process. The Member entity has an outstandingFines balance. A business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books until they pay. The FinePayment creates a transaction record and reduces the balance. Like fee calculation in parking lots, I use BigDecimal for money — double arithmetic has floating-point precision issues that would make accounting incorrect.

follow_up_questions: What if a member disputes a fine — how would you handle that in the design?
Should fines be calculated lazily (on return) or eagerly (each day)?

StandardFineCalculator: DAILY_RATE times max(0, overdueDays) — zero if returned on time
Member entity tracks outstandingFines balance
Business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books

beats.text: FineCalculator is a Strategy: StandardFineCalculator, WeekdayOnlyFineCalculator, or GracePeriodFineCalculator can all plug in without changing the checkout process.

production trap: use BigDecimal for fine amounts — never double. Floating-point rounding errors compound in financial calculations and would make accounting incorrect. This is true for any money calculation in Java.

sections.title: Fine Calculation with Temporal Logic
sections.content: **Fine calculation** is triggered when a Member returns a BookItem. The system compares the **return date** to the **due date** stored in the BookLending record. If the return date is after the due date, the member owes a fine. The basic formula: **fine = overdue days × daily rate**. Overdue days is calculated using Java's **ChronoUnit.DAYS.between()** for precision. However, real libraries have nuances: a **grace period** (first day free), **weekend/holiday exclusion** (fines don't accrue on non-business days), and **progressive rates** (first week at $1/day, second week at $2/day). Use the **Strategy pattern** for FineCalculator to encapsulate these rules. Different member types (standard, student, premium) might have different rates. The calculated fine is added to the Member's **outstanding balance**. Before issuing a new book, the system checks if the member has unpaid fines and blocks borrowing until they're cleared. This enforces financial accountability. The analogy: fines are like parking tickets—calculated based on violation duration, accumulate until paid, and prevent you from registering a new vehicle if unpaid.

sections.title: Fine Calculation with Strategy Pattern
Key Points
content: **Temporal calculation**: Use ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(dueDate, returnDate) for accurate day counting. Avoid manual date arithmetic which misses leap years and daylight saving.
**Grace period**: Real libraries often forgive the first day or two overdue. Subtract grace days before applying the rate to avoid penalizing minor delays.
**Progressive rates**: Fines can escalate—first week at lower rate, second week higher. ProgressiveFineCalculator encapsulates this tiered logic.
**BigDecimal for money**: Always use BigDecimal for financial calculations, never double or float. Avoids rounding errors that compound in monetary transactions.
**Outstanding balance tracking**: Member entity stores cumulative fines. Before issuing a book, check member.canBorrow() which verifies zero outstanding balance.
**Strategy pattern for rates**: Different member types (student, senior, premium) have different fine rates. FineCalculator interface allows injecting the appropriate strategy.
**Fine as transaction**: Create a Fine entity to record when, why, and how much was charged. Essential for audit trail and dispute resolution.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd calculate fines during the book return process. When a member returns a BookItem, the system looks at the BookLending record which has the due date. It compares that to the actual return date using ChronoUnit.DAYS.between to get the overdue days. If the book is returned on time or early, no fine is charged. If it's late, the basic formula is overdue days times the daily rate. However, I'd add a grace period—say the first day is free to account for minor delays. That's a common library practice. For the calculation logic, I'd use the Strategy pattern with a FineCalculator interface. That lets you have different rate structures. For example, StandardFineCalculator charges one dollar per day, but ProgressiveFineCalculator could charge one dollar for the first week and two dollars per day after that. Student members might get a discounted rate. Importantly, I'd use BigDecimal for all money calculations, never double, to avoid rounding errors. The calculated fine gets added to the Member's outstanding balance. Before allowing the member to borrow again, the system checks if their balance is zero. If they have unpaid fines, borrowing is blocked until they pay. The common mistake is forgetting to block future borrowing or miscalculating days by using simple subtraction instead of proper date APIs. You'd also want to create a Fine entity to record each charge for audit purposes, not just update a number.

questions.question: What are the key design decisions in the library management system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you articulate design rationale and justify architectural choices, showing understanding of trade-offs and pattern selection criteria
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers list design patterns without explaining why they were chosen or fail to connect decisions to real library operations and scalability needs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly mention trade-offs for each decision and alternative approaches you considered, showing depth of analysis beyond pattern matching

questions.direct_answer: Key decisions: separate Book (catalog) from BookItem (physical copy) for inventory tracking, use Queue for FIFO reservation fairness, apply Strategy pattern for extensible search and fine calculation, implement Observer pattern for return notifications, and define role-based permissions with Member versus Librarian classes for access control.

answer_sections.content: The design decisions I'm most deliberate about: Book vs BookItem — the hardest part for beginners is realizing a library book has two representations. Without this separation, you can't track which physical copy is where or handle multiple copies. Reservation queue as a Queue (FIFO) — because reservation fairness matters: first come, first served. Strategy for FineCalculator — libraries change their fine policies, so this needs to be swappable. Observer for notifications — when a book is available, the right member needs to know; Observer decouples the availability tracking from notification logic. Role separation between Member and Librarian: Librarian can add books, block members, adjust fines; Member can search and borrow. These could be separate classes or role-based permissions.

sections.title: Architectural Decisions and Rationale
sections.content: Designing a library management system requires making **intentional trade-offs** between simplicity and real-world fidelity. The first major decision is **Book versus BookItem separation**: one class for catalog metadata, another for physical inventory. This mirrors how libraries actually work—one title, many copies—and enables tracking each copy's status independently. The **Queue for reservations** ensures FIFO fairness: members are served in request order, not randomly or by status. The **Strategy pattern** appears twice: for search criteria (title, author, ISBN) and fine calculation (standard, progressive rates). This keeps the system extensible without modifying core classes. The **Observer pattern** decouples return processing from reservation notifications: when a BookItem returns, it doesn't directly manage reservations; instead, it notifies the Book, which processes its queue. Finally, **role-based access** with Member and Librarian classes enforces permissions: members can borrow and reserve, librarians can issue books and manage inventory. Each decision trades complexity for flexibility—a simpler design might merge entities or hardcode search logic, but it wouldn't scale as requirements evolve.

sections.title: Design Decisions Reflected in Code Structure
Key Points
content: **Book-BookItem separation rationale**: One catalog entry can have multiple physical copies. Without separation, you can't track that copy A is loaned while copy B is available.
**Queue for fairness**: FIFO ensures first requester gets the book first. Alternative (notify all) creates race conditions. Queue is simpler and fairer.
**Strategy for extensibility**: Hardcoded search methods (searchByTitle, searchByAuthor) bloat the catalog class. Strategy lets you add new searches without modifying existing code.
**Observer for decoupling**: BookItem doesn't know about reservations. It notifies Book on return, and Book processes the queue. Separation of concerns keeps classes focused.
**Role-based access**: Member and Librarian have different capabilities. Prevents members from adding books to inventory or waiving fines—operations only librarians should perform.
**Trade-off: complexity vs flexibility**: These patterns add classes and indirection. For a tiny library (100 books), overkill. For a city library (100K books), essential for maintainability.
**Alternative rejected**: Flat design with one Book class containing availability boolean. Simpler but breaks when you need per-copy tracking, reservations, or multi-copy inventory.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The first key decision is separating Book from BookItem. Book represents the catalog entry—title, author, ISBN—while BookItem is each physical copy with its own barcode and location. I chose this because one book title can have five copies on different shelves with independent availability. Without separation, you can't model that. The trade-off is extra complexity, but it matches real library operations. Second decision is using a Queue for reservations. When all copies are loaned, members join a waiting list. A queue ensures FIFO fairness—first to reserve gets the book first. I considered notifying all waiting members and letting them race, but that's unfair and creates contention. The queue is simpler and guarantees order. Third, I use the Strategy pattern in two places: search criteria and fine calculation. For search, instead of hardcoding searchByTitle and searchByAuthor methods in the catalog, I define a SearchCriteria interface. Each search type is a separate class. This keeps the catalog clean and lets you add new searches without modifying existing code. Same logic for fine calculation—different member types might have different rates, so FineCalculator is pluggable. Fourth is the Observer pattern for return notifications. When a BookItem is returned, it doesn't directly check reservations—that'd be tight coupling. Instead, it notifies its parent Book, which processes the reservation queue. This decouples inventory operations from reservation logic. Finally, role-based access with Member and Librarian classes. Members can borrow and reserve. Librarians can issue books and manage inventory. This enforces permissions—you don't want members adding books to the system. The common mistake is listing patterns without explaining why or skipping the trade-offs. Every decision has a cost. These patterns add classes, but they make the system maintainable as requirements grow.
